commits.message:
feat(comm): wire the already-running RabbitMQ/Redis into the intake path

Closes the three gaps flagged since COMM's first documentation pass:
no queueing, no retry, no idempotency. RabbitMQ and Redis have been
running on this host, unused, since the service was first deployed --
this wires them in rather than standing up anything new.

Idempotency (comm_gateway/idempotency.py): a Redis SETNX+EX claim on
(channel, source_message_id) before anything else happens. Telegram
retries a webhook on timeout; a retried delivery is now acknowledged
without being re-processed or re-queued, closing the exact gap
HERMES-450 already documented as intended (dedup by channel +
source_message_id) one hop earlier, before the message even reaches
Hermes.

Queue topology (comm_gateway/queue.py): comm.intake (exchange) ->
comm.intake.telegram (queue) is the main path. Retry uses a
delayed-requeue pattern with no plugin dependency: a failed message
goes to comm.intake.retry -> comm.intake.telegram.retry with a
per-message `expiration` set to an exponential backoff delay
(5s/15s/60s/300s/900s); that queue's own dead-letter-exchange points
back at the main queue, so RabbitMQ redelivers it automatically once
the delay elapses. After 5 attempts (COMM_MAX_RETRIES), a message goes
to comm.intake.dead for manual inspection instead of retrying forever.

Worker (comm_gateway/worker.py): a new process, same image as
comm-gateway, different entrypoint (`python -m comm_gateway.worker`,
new comm-worker service in docker-compose.yml). Consumes the intake
queue, calls Hermes, delivers the Telegram reply -- the same functions
main.py used to call inline. Retry policy distinguishes definitive
failures (401/403/404/422 -- the identical payload will never succeed
differently) from transient ones (5xx, or hermes_client.py's
timeout/connection-error/blocked shape) -- only the latter get retried;
the former go straight to the dead-letter queue with the user still
notified immediately.

main.py's webhook handler changed shape accordingly: it now claims the
idempotency key, normalizes, publishes to the queue, and acks Telegram
immediately (`{"status": "queued"}`) instead of waiting on the full
Hermes round-trip inline. A startup hook declares the queue topology
so it exists even if the worker container hasn't started yet.

Verified: scripts/comm-queue-retry-check.py (topology declares cleanly,
idempotency actually dedups, retry-vs-dead-letter classification
matches the policy for all three cases -- non-retryable, retryable,
and exhausted-retries) passes against the live containers. A real
end-to-end webhook call was sent through the deployed pipeline: queued
-> worker consumed it -> Hermes call succeeded (200) -> Telegram send
attempted (400, expected -- the test used a fake chat_id, not a real
recipient). A second identical delivery correctly returned
{"status": "duplicate"} without re-processing.

Incident, found and fixed in the same pass: the worker's initial
logging.basicConfig(level=INFO) caused httpx's own request logger to
emit full request URLs, and Telegram's Bot API embeds the live bot
token directly in the URL path -- this leaked the token into
`docker logs jobfynder-comm-worker` once, in this session's own
testing. Fixed by setting httpx/httpcore's loggers to WARNING
specifically rather than lowering the root logger; confirmed a repeat
webhook test produces zero token occurrences in the logs. The one
container-log file that had the leaked token was gone after the
recreate (Docker's json-file driver uses a per-container-ID file, and
no external log shipping was found configured for this host) --
checked directly on disk, nothing found. Not otherwise remediated
(rotating the bot token itself requires BotFather/Telegram-side
access this session doesn't have); flagged as a recommendation, not
forced through, since the practical exposure was bounded to whoever
already has SSH+docker access to this host -- the same trust boundary
as reading .env directly.
